content: Pelargonium sidoides, also known as Umckaloabo, is a herbal remedy that has been proposed as a treatment for acute respiratory infections (ARIs). The aim of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of Pelargonium sidoides in managing ARIs in both children and adults. A comprehensive search was conducted in April 2013 across multiple databases, including MEDLINE, The Cochrane Library, EMBASE, and others, as well as clinical trial registries such as ClinicalTrials.gov and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform. The inclusion criteria were double-blind, randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared Pelargonium sidoides preparations to placebo or other treatments. The primary outcome was the complete resolution of all symptoms, with additional analysis of predefined key symptoms. Data extraction and quality assessment were performed independently by at least two reviewers. Separate analyses were conducted based on age groups and specific disease entities. Subgroup analyses considered the type of preparation (liquid or tablets). Statistical heterogeneity was assessed using the I² statistic, and pooled risk ratios (RR) were calculated using either fixed-effect or random-effects models, depending on the level of heterogeneity. Out of 10 eligible studies, eight were included in the analysis, while two were excluded due to insufficient quality. Three trials involving 746 adult patients with acute bronchitis demonstrated that the liquid preparation of Pelargonium sidoides was effective for most outcomes, whereas the tablet form was not. Similarly, three trials involving 819 children with acute bronchitis showed comparable results, with the liquid preparation being effective. However, due to significant heterogeneity related to the type of preparation, pooled analyses were not performed for these studies. One study involving 103 adults with sinusitis showed significant treatment effects, with complete symptom resolution by day 21 (RR 0.43, 95% CI 0.30 to 0.62), although the quality of evidence was rated as very low. Another study on the common cold demonstrated efficacy after 10 days of treatment but not after five days, also with very low-quality evidence. The overall quality of the included studies was rated as moderate, with limitations such as unvalidated outcome assessments, minor attrition issues, and the fact that all trials were investigator-initiated. A funnel plot suggested the possibility of publication bias. Adverse events were more frequently reported in the Pelargonium sidoides groups compared to placebo, but none were classified as serious. In conclusion, Pelargonium sidoides may provide symptom relief for acute rhinosinusitis and the common cold in adults, though uncertainty remains. It may also be effective for acute bronchitis in both adults and children, as well as sinusitis in adults. However, the overall quality of evidence was low for acute bronchitis and very low for sinusitis and the common cold. No reliable data were available for other types of acute respiratory infections.
